headline: Ward 3's absentee-ownership number is the one ranking here that isn't part of a crowd.
summary:
Eighty-five percent of the residential parcels in this ward list a taxpayer mailing address that isn't the property itself, the worst share of any of Chicago's fifty wards, a ranking with no caveat attached anywhere in the data. Right below it sits a related number, the share of rent that ends up as landlord profit rather than mortgage payoff, modeled two separate ways, once against each home's assessed value and once against its actual sale price. Both formulas land on 69.8 percent, the same figure to three decimal places, and both rank 47th of 50. The write-up counts that as two separate weaknesses, but it's one finding measured two different ways.

The ward's best marks split a similar way. Ward 3 places third on parks and on both 311 turnaround clocks. The parks count comes with no caveat at all, while the two 311 times carry a note that the underlying measure is not fully populated across the fifty wards. The two historic-preservation counts that look most impressive, National Register listings and official city landmarks, are ranked against smaller pools of 41 and 43 wards instead, because that data simply wasn't collected for the other nine and seven. A developer's long-delayed plan to build a grocery store, a hardware store, and new apartments on the old Stateway Gardens site would add still more units to a housing stock where 85 out of every 100 homes already answer to an owner who lives somewhere else.
reading_the_rankings: Two rankings here are easy to misread. Ward 3 ranks second in the city on a count of congregations rated 4.8 or higher with at least 25 reviews, 12 of them here, but the different measure just below it, how many distinct religious traditions those congregations represent, lands near the bottom at 47th. Highly rated and varied are different questions, and this ward only answers one of them well. The other easy misread is 48th place on menu-spending spread, how evenly the alderperson's own capital budget reaches every block instead of clustering in one corner. That number is a record of one office's spending choices rather than a fact about the neighborhood, and part of the trend behind it belongs to a ward whose lines got redrawn in 2023.

news.headline: Long-Delayed Plans For Bronzeville Pete's Fresh Market To Go Before City Panel Next Month
news.note: A developer plans to bring a grocery store, hardware store and apartments to the former Stateway Gardens site in Bronzeville, with a city Plan Commission hearing set for August 20.

news.headline: After Young People Shot In Bronzeville, Alder Calls For Accountability Over Teen Gatherings
news.note: Seven young people were shot in two separate incidents in Bronzeville over one weekend, prompting calls for parents and social media platforms to address unsanctioned teen gatherings.

news.headline: South Loop Neighbors Pitch New Bus Connector As Development Booms In Area
news.note: A community group proposed a 4.2-mile CTA bus route through the South Loop to ease congestion tied to nearby development, including the new Chicago Fire stadium.
